topic.title: Destination wedding filter
topic.claim: A destination wedding isn't about the view; it's a polite way to shrink the guest list without uninviting anyone.
topic.moment: The Udaipur wedding where half the relatives 'just couldn't make it.'

turn.believed: The couple wanted a scenic, special celebration.
turn.actually: Distance and cost quietly remove the guests you didn't want, and nobody has to be cut.

topic.because: Flights and three-night stays do the filtering for you. The people who won't spend are exactly the ones you were never close to anyway.
topic.payoff: A destination wedding is the softest 'you're not invited' ever invented.
topic.behaviour: Families pick far-off venues partly to keep numbers and obligations down.
topic.mechanism: The airfare cuts the guest list so the host doesn't have to.
topic.group: Couples and families planning weddings, and the relatives who feel the distance
topic.send_to: A cousin planning a 'small intimate' wedding somewhere expensive.
topic.why_now: Destination weddings keep rising and the guest lists keep shrinking.

cover.headline: A destination wedding [uninvites] the relatives you didn't want
cover.sub: Half of them 'just couldn't make it.' Funny, which half.

paragraphs: A destination wedding isn't really about the view. It removes the guests you didn't want, and nobody ever has to say so.
slides.why_swipe: How does a venue remove guests? The reader wants the trick.

paragraphs: The wedding is in Udaipur. Three nights at a hotel by the lake, flights for two, sometimes four.
And suddenly half the relatives 'just couldn't make it.' Work came up. Kids' exams. Something always comes up.
slides.why_swipe: Why did exactly those people drop out, and not the others?

paragraphs: Everyone says the couple wanted something scenic. Nice photos, a break from the usual banquet hall near home.
But look at who vanished. **It's never the inner circle. It's always the far edge of the family.**
slides.why_swipe: What makes the far edge drop out so neatly?

paragraphs: A flight and three nights cost real money. The people who won't spend it are, almost always, the ones you were never close to.
So the ticket price sorts the list for you. No one is told anything. They just do the maths and stay home.
slides.why_swipe: If nobody is cut, who actually walks away happy?

paragraphs: And the couple comes out clean. They get the smaller crowd and the lower bill, without making one awkward call.
No aunty is told she wasn't wanted. She removes herself, politely, over a WhatsApp 'beta, itni door yaar.' The lake is just the alibi.
slides.why_swipe: So what should you actually watch for in your own plans?

paragraphs: So before you book that fort on a hill, ask yourself one thing.
**The guests you're secretly hoping can't afford it are the ones this whole plan was for.**

end.save: Open this again the next time a 'small, intimate' wedding somewhere expensive lands in your chats.
end.send: Send to a cousin planning a 'small intimate' wedding in a hill fort.

draft.caption: Think about the last destination wedding you skipped. Was it the flight, or did you both already know you weren't that close?
draft.alt_text: A six-slide text post arguing that a destination wedding is a polite way to shrink the guest list. Because flights and a three-night stay cost money, the relatives the couple was never close to quietly stay home, so the host controls the numbers and the budget without ever uninviting anyone.
